turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, Lerato, I'm just going to pop the cuff on before the doctor comes through. Sit however is comfy.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, thanks, my hands are a bit cold from the aircon, and we got stuck at the robot on Main for ages, so I'm flustered, but that's not really why I'm here. The actual thing is this fluttering in my chest.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, pulse ninety-six, sats ninety-eight percent, and you're breathing at sixteen. I'll leave the file, Doctor's just battling with the computer.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen has frozen again. What can I do for you today, the reception note is tiny.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): My heart keeps racing and pounding, like it skips and then sprints, mostly when I'm lying in bed at night, and also before a work meeting or an exam for this part-time course. I'm twenty-four, I work in marketing in town, and we live in a flat in Observatory. I don't think I'm a stressy person, hey, I actually cope very well, I just like being prepared.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She does that sitting-up thing at night. I'm Kyle, I stay with her. It's been every night for about three weeks, and you bolt upright and say you can't get air.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the cursor jumped, say the timing again, I only half heard. And you said breathless as well?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, not every night, and it's not three weeks, it's been going on for months. It started around the June block exams, or maybe the September ones, I honestly can't pin the date. The breathlessness comes with the pounding, worse at night and just before I present at work or write a test, but it's not stress, I thrive on a deadline.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ag, Lerato, you were up till three before that client pitch. You told me your chest felt tight. That's stress, whether you call it that or not.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say tight like pain, there isn't pain, I just meant the air wasn't moving. I'm not anxious. I had one flat white this morning and I chat a lot because that's how I talk, not because I'm panicking in this room.

[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay, so I'm hearing anything from about three weeks on Kyle's side to a few months on yours, and we won't pin the start date. Any actual pain in the chest, or pain going to the arm or jaw?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and no pain down the arm, nothing like that. I've gone over it because my uncle had a heart attack, but that was him, he was sixty and smoked proper cigarettes.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you blacked out, or felt like you were going to faint?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never fainted, never even greyed out. I stay awake and I just lie there counting the beats, then I lose count because my brain hops to the slide deck.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, let me click this. Coffee, energy drinks, the note says something but I can't read my typing.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, about four flat whites a day, sometimes five if the afternoon is hectic, and usually two energy drinks, Monster or the cheap Dragon ones from the garage. I don't drink alcohol really, maybe a cider at a braai once in a while, not weekly. And I vape, watermelon ice disposables, pretty much from waking until I sleep.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's more than two Monsters some days, I've seen three in the recycling. And the vape is in her hand in the car, at the robot, everywhere.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say the vaping bit again, an email popped up over the screen.

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Watermelon ice disposable, all day, every day, for about two years. I switched off cigarettes at varsity, I only smoked for about a year, maybe three a day, and then I stopped the cigarettes completely. The vape I have not stopped.
[SEG0020] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to stick my head in, the ECG machine is free after this consult if you want it. I'll be in the next cubicle.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sharp, thanks, we'll use it. Any cough, wheeze, sputum, or fevers?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough, no wheeze, no fever, no green stuff. The breathing thing is only with the heart racing, not like a cold, and I can walk up to the flat fine if my heart is quiet.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you actually taking, including the chemist stuff?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The big chalky magnesium tablets from Clicks, two at night, for the calf cramps and because some article said it calms palpitations, though I forget them half the time. Panado extra strength when a headache shows up, I swallow maybe a thousand milligrams, and I'm not a hundred percent sure of that dose. I was on the little white heart tablet, propranolol, for the racing, I thought forty milligrams but no, sorry, it was ten milligrams twice a day, and I stopped it. They offered me Cipralex at student health and I never took a single tablet.

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So magnesium two at night, but you miss doses, and the white tablet was propranolol ten milligrams twice a day, stopped. When did you stop it, this screen wants a date and I haven't got one.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, I stopped it last winter, or the winter before that, I can't tell you the month. It made my hands cold and I felt flat, so I just left it in the cupboard, I didn't wean. The Cipralex bottle I never even opened.

[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): While you're on families, her sister has an underactive thyroid and she takes Eltroxin every morning, the sister does, not Lerato. My mate at work eats biotin gummies for her hair, and that's got nothing to do with us.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, Thandi, my older sister, she's been on Eltroxin for years, that's her script, and I have never taken thyroid medicine. I don't have a thyroid diagnosis, I just google too much because her numbers were off and now my heart is weird.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no allergies, I can take Panado and penicillin and nothing happens. My sister gets a rash from something but I don't even know what, and that's her, not me.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, allergies again, the dropdown jumped. None at all?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): None. No drug allergies and no food allergies.

[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She also gets calf cramps at night, that's why the magnesium, she didn't say how sore they are. The headaches are like once or twice a week, behind the eyes, not a migraine I don't think.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the cramps are real, both calves, at night, for a few months as well, and they ease if I walk around the flat. Headaches maybe twice a week, behind the eyes, not killing me, and the Panado takes the edge off, no lights and no vomiting.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while this thing loads. Heart sounds are normal, rhythm is regular, just a bit quick, same as the nurse's pulse, chest is clear with no wheeze and no crackles, and the calves are soft, not hot, not swollen.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The quick pulse is probably the flat white and power-walking from the parking because we were late, loadshedding killed the alarm, sorry, that's a tangent. I don't feel it racing right this second the way I do at night.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to start a new tablet today. My working impression is this is most likely the caffeine, the vape, and the adrenaline before meetings and exams, even if you don't want to call it stress. I still can't rule out an overactive thyroid or an abnormal rhythm, so those stay on the list.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're not saying my heart is failing, because I read about cardiomyopathy at one in the morning and that was a mistake. I can stop reading, I just need to know you're not brushing me off because I talk a lot.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not brushing you off. We'll do an ECG today, Sister can do it just now, and bloods for TSH and free T4. No echo unless those come back odd.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Can she still do the pitch on Thursday, or should she call in sick?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): She can work. Before the meeting, try breathing exercises, in for four counts, hold for four, out for six, a few rounds. And cut the energy drinks right down, and the coffee, and ease off the vape if you can, that's on you, not a script.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): In for four, hold four, out for six, I can do that in the car at the robot. Cutting Monster will be harder than the breathing, I'm not going to pretend. I'll try with the vape, but I'm not promising zero.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks for the results. If the palpitations get worse before then, or you faint, come back sooner, don't wait the two weeks.
[SEG0044] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the thyroid bloods at the lab downstairs and do the ECG in the side room once you're done. The ECG is the sticky dots, five minutes, no needle for that one.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I had an ECG in matric after I fainted at netball, but that was dehydration, they said the tracing was normal, and I haven't fainted since. I don't want you to think I faint now, that was years ago, a once-off.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Say that fainting again? Matric, once, normal ECG, nothing since?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, once, in matric, hot day, netball, they said dehydration, and the ECG was normal. Nothing since, and I shouldn't have said never earlier, I just forgot about school.
[SEG0048] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I didn't know about the netball thing. She's not fainting now, that I can swear to.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good, past faint, not part of this episode. Keep the magnesium if the cramps like it, even if you miss doses, don't start your sister's Eltroxin or anyone's biotin, and leave the propranolol stopped, we're not restarting it today.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, two weeks, breathing counts, less Monster, ECG sticky dots, thyroid bloods. I'll try to write down the nights it happens so I'm not so vague next time, and thanks for putting up with the long version.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pleasure. Sister will call you in just now, and go easy on the vape in the parking lot.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Denied blacking out/feeling faint currently: patient said she has never fainted or even greyed out during these current episodes, despite one remote faint in matric only.

Breathlessness occurs only together with the heart racing, and she can walk up to the flat fine when her heart is quiet.
Energy drink intake may exceed the patient's estimate: caregiver reported more than two Monsters on some days, having seen three in the recycling.
Current caffeine on the day of review included one flat white that morning.
Patient reported vaping 'pretty much from waking until I sleep' / 'all day, every day' for about two years.
Patient had been offered Cipralex (escitalopram) previously but never took a single tablet / never opened the bottle.
Reason propranolol was stopped: it made her hands cold and she felt flat; she stopped it without weaning.
Magnesium indication included calf cramps specifically, and she forgets the tablets about half the time.
Panado was specifically Extra Strength, and the stated 1000 mg dose was uncertain.
Medication allergy details: patient specifically stated no drug allergies and no food allergies, and that penicillin causes no reaction.
Additional headache negatives: headaches are not migraine-like.
